planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Farrer is pistillate (female-flowered) and needs a self-fertile muscadine such as Carlos or Cowart within about 50 feet to set fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis strong enough to carry a vigorous vine for decades. Farrer produces large, elongated, purple berries that are notably sweeter than the older Jumbo cultivar, ripening early to mid-September with high sugar content that makes them a favorite for out-of-hand eating. Because the vine is female-flowered only, it will not fruit reliably on its own and should be interplanted with a self-fertile black or bronze muscadine for pollination. Prune hard each winter back to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest berries individually as they loosen from the cluster rather than waiting for the whole bunch to drop.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Florida Fry is self-fertile and well suited to North Florida, South Alabama, and the wider Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, training the vine onto an overhead arbor or high-wire trellis as it establishes over its first two to three years. Florida Fry bears large, golden-bronze berries with a dry stem scar that ripen early to mid-season, and unlike the older Fry cultivar it does not require a separate pollinizer vine to produce a full crop. The sweet, musky fruit is primarily grown for fresh eating but also works well in preserves and homemade wine. Keep the root zone mulched and irrigated during fruit swell, and prune back to short spurs each dormant season to maintain fruiting wood and airflow through the canopy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Florida
University of Florida IFAS Extension — HS100/HS763 The Muscadine Grape

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; African Queen is pistillate (female-flowered) and needs a self-fertile black muscadine nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a strong overhead arbor, since this is a vigorous grower that needs sturdy support. African Queen was bred from a Sugargate by Dixieland cross and produces large, uniformly ripening black berries with very high sugar content and a dry stem scar that holds well after picking. Because the vine carries only female flowers, it sets little to no fruit without a self-fertile pollinizer such as Cowart or Carlos planted within pollination range. The vine is notably disease resistant and productive, making it a dependable mid-season black muscadine once paired correctly; prune to short spurs each winter and harvest as berries loosen from the cluster.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Creek is self-fertile, so a single vine will set a full crop without a separate pollinizer.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a high-wire trellis or overhead arbor strong enough to support a long-lived, vigorous vine. Creek is one of the older University of Georgia breeding-program releases and remains available today as a self-fertile, late-ripening muscadine bearing sweet purple-black berries that carry noticeably more acidity than most other cultivars. That extra acid balances its sugar well, making Creek a popular choice both for fresh eating off the vine and for home muscadine winemaking. Prune back hard each dormant season to short spurs on permanent cordons, and expect this late-season variety to extend the harvest window after earlier-ripening cultivars have finished.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grape Breeding history
